rounds.text: Supreme Facility Management Ltd trades at an exceptionally low P/E of 4.11x [E1] and a P/B of 0.47x [E2], representing a massive discount to sector benchmarks where the P/E sits at 18.1x and the P/B at 1.38x [E6, E7]. This deep undervaluation stands in stark contrast to the company's robust operational expansion, demonstrated by a 5-year compounded sales growth of 23% and a trailing twelve-month compounded profit growth of 34% [E14, E19]. Furthermore, the intrinsic value derived from a discounted cash flow model points to ₹ 131 per share against a current market price of ₹ 18.4, offering a striking margin of safety of 86.0% [E39, E40]. Reverse DCF analysis confirms that the market price irrationally prices in a -9.8% earnings decline, ignoring the company's actual delivery of strong 31.8% CAGR profit growth over the last 5 years [E41, E46]. Domestic institutional investors have recognized this disconnect, increasing their stake significantly from 1.42% to 5.25% [E37], while promoters maintain a high and stable holding at 71.52% [E35]. Conceded: debt-to-equity stands at an elevated 1.51x alongside a negative free cash flow of Rs -36 Cr in Mar 2026 [E30, E31].

Despite apparent statistical cheapness, Supreme Facility Management Ltd (SFML) harbors severe balance sheet and cash flow risks that undermine its low valuation multiples. Most critically, the company generated a staggering negative free cash flow of Rs -36 Cr in March 2026 [E30], which severely contrasts with its reported operating cash flow of Rs 7 Cr [E29] and highlights major capital burn. This cash drain is accompanied by escalating debt, with total borrowings climbing from Rs 116 Cr to Rs 146 Cr in March 2026 [E33], pushing the debt-to-equity ratio to a concerning 1.51x where debt exceeds net worth [E31]. Furthermore, the company struggles with a low interest coverage ratio [E48] and an inconsistent yearly and quarterly operating-margin trend [E26, E27]. Market participants are taking note of these underlying pressures, as evidenced by a 56% drop in the share price over the past year [E20], the stock sitting merely 7% above its 52-week low [E5], negative institutional money flow [E38], and a complete exit by foreign institutions down to 0.00% [E36]. Conceded: the company boasts a low P/E of 4.11x [E1], a price-to-book ratio of 0.47x [E2], and solid historical sales and profit growth [E14, E17].

Conceded: free cash flow was negative at Rs -36 Cr in March 2026 [E30], borrowings increased to Rs 146 Cr [E33], and the debt-to-equity ratio sits at 1.51x [E31]. However, the business maintains a positive operating cash flow of Rs 7 Cr [E29] and an adequate current ratio of 1.67x [E32]. The bear's focus on share price performance (-56% over 1 year) [E20] and the 52-week range position [E5] completely ignores the fundamental disconnect with intrinsic value, where a DCF model calculates a massive margin of safety of 86.0% [E40] at an intrinsic value of Rs 131 per share against a market price of Rs 18.4 [E39]. Furthermore, the reverse DCF indicates that the current market price aggressively prices in -9.8% earnings growth, which directly contradicts the company's actual historical performance of 31.8% CAGR profit growth over 5 years [E41, E46]. While foreign institutions exited [E36], domestic institutions have increased their stake from 1.42% to 5.25% [E37], demonstrating tangible institutional confidence that overrides the bear's narrow reading of capital flows.

Conceded: domestic institutions increased their stake to 5.25% [E37]. However, the bull's dismissal of capital health ignores the alarming plunge of free cash flow to negative Rs 36 Cr and the escalation of borrowings to Rs 146 Cr, which leave the debt-to-equity ratio at a precarious 1.51x [E30, E31, E33]. The reliance on a DCF model projecting an intrinsic value of Rs 131 completely clashes with the reality of negative money flow and a zero dividend yield [E4, E38, E39]. Furthermore, citing historical profit growth fails to counter the flagged negatives of a low interest coverage ratio, a suspicious tax rate, and decelerating earnings growth [E48, E49, E56]. Foreign institutions have entirely exited the stock at 0.00%, confirming that institutional money flow is negative [E36, E38]. Finally, the 56% collapse in share price over the past year is not an arbitrary disconnect, but a reflection of these severe fundamental strains [E20].
